lesson.title: Negative Reinforcement: Removing Something to Build a Habit
lesson.summary: Negative reinforcement means removing an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior in order to make that behavior more likely to happen again.
lesson.body:
Negative reinforcement is where the terminology trips people up the most, largely because negative sounds like it should mean something bad is happening to the organism. It does not. Negative here simply means something is being taken away, and reinforcement, as always, means the behavior becomes more likely afterward. So negative reinforcement is the removal of an aversive, unpleasant stimulus following a behavior, and that removal is what makes the behavior more likely to occur again.

A familiar example: a car's seatbelt alarm beeps repeatedly and annoyingly until the driver buckles the seatbelt, at which point the beeping stops. The unpleasant sound is removed, and drivers become more likely to buckle up quickly in the future specifically to make that sound go away. Taking a painkiller to relieve a headache works the same way: the pain, the aversive stimulus, is removed once the medication takes effect, which makes taking that painkiller the next time a headache strikes more likely.

It helps to keep negative reinforcement and punishment firmly separate, since they are easy to mix up. Negative reinforcement is still, unambiguously, a form of reinforcement: it makes the preceding behavior more likely, not less. What is removed is something unpleasant to the organism, and that removal is what strengthens the behavior, the opposite outcome of any form of punishment, which is covered next.
